extracted.intended_audience: journalists, reporters, and newsroom editors seeking to practice constructive journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Practical handbook guidance for planning, researching, interviewing, storytelling, and implementing constructive journalism in newsrooms — focusing on solutions, nuances, and democratic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: AVIS-K news criteria (Timeliness, Importance, Identification, Sensation, Conflict)
rubrics_metrics.description: Danish tool AVIS-K: five news criteria used to identify and produce 'a good story' — Timeliness, Importance, Identification, Sensation, and Conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traditional criteria are widely used but have limitations; many outlets complement or modify them to include constructive approaches that build trust, strengthen democratic dialogue, and foster community cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim: Contribute to democracy through critical constructive journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching aim: to contribute to democracy by complementing watchdog journalism with constructive approaches — promoting democratic conversation and suggesting solutions, while maintaining critical research and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive journalism should remain rigorous and critical; it is an additional editorial resource to be used appropriately to strengthen public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on solutions (Pillar 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a problem with known consequences and look for possible solutions; approach solutions with the same critical scrutiny as problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a replicable, scalable solution is identified, present findings to those responsible, follow up to see if the issue was resolved. Key questions: How do we move forward? Who has solved a similar problem? Does it work everywhere? Who can solve it? Do stakeholders offer a solution? Should a new solution be developed? Can we help citizens and experts find or develop solutions together?

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on overview and nuances (Pillar 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with context and nuances by analyzing development over time, comprehensive data, and multiple perspectives to provide a deeper understanding of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek data and facts that provide an overview; ask: Which data can offer deeper understanding? Could additional sources reveal nuances? How has the issue developed over time? What is the historical background and wider context? Are there stories to revisit? Are there myths to confirm or refute?

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic Conversation / Involvement (Pillar 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate and develop ideas by involving citizens, stakeholders, experts, and decision-makers — adopting public-powered journalism and dialogue journalism to facilitate debate and bridge divides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to involve citizens before or after story development; consider live events, workshops, debates. Key questions: Can our media involve relevant actors? Should involvement be before or after story identification? Can we engage the audience to develop solutions, nuance the story, or build bridges?

rubrics_metrics.name: Research for solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When researching a solution, analyze critically: evidence of effect, reasons it works here, replication elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key checks: Is the solution scalable? Does it work in other places? Can experts/researchers validate it? Who is responsible? Who can work with it? How and when could it be used? Will decision-makers use it? Maintain critical scrutiny equal to that used in investigating problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research for nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: Search broadly and deeply for sources and data that complicate or add subtlety beyond a simplistic 'he said / she said' model, aiming to present the most accurate picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What does an overview of all available data show? How does data reflect normality vs extremes? How do findings compare to other debates? What has developed over years and why? Who is responsible for developments? Who or what explains the problem from different sides? Is it better or worse than before? Why now?

rubrics_metrics.name: Research with engagement (public-powered journalism & post-choice engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage citizens either before choosing the story (to surface public agenda) or after choosing the story (to extend shelf life and access new knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before: ask what is on the public agenda; what do citizens wonder about? After: decide whether to engage broadly or with key stakeholders; be clear about the engagement goal (wider perspective, mediation, explore solutions). Questions: What are the most important challenges? How to engage stakeholders and who has power to make changes?

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive selection of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Include voices representing all sides and those that add solutions or nuances; ensure sources reflect the population's composition, include those with lived experience and experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to source credibility, special interests/motives, status (party affiliation, experience, expertise), representativeness, and occupational/privacy-related bias. Avoid reproducing stereotypes and 'parachute journalism' that reduces regions/communities to narrow themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding false balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lend equal weight to unsupported opinion when evidence favors one side; identify and emphasize the strongest evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one side lacks data and relies on opinion, giving both equal space creates false balance. Instead, reveal complexities, identify strongest evidence, and avoid endorsing unsupported arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of framing and language choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that angle, source selection, and word choice shape audience perception; framing is an unconscious subjective process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose language carefully and accurately. Avoid presenting sources as helpless victims or seeking extremes/worst cases. Counter lazy stereotypes by selecting courageous, determined examples that might inspire solutions. Questions to avoid framing: How are we framing the story/actors? Are we aware of our own bias? Do we ask questions without prejudice? Is the case representative? Is the case portrayed as helpless or energetic? Are selection criteria neutral?

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive interview technique — avoid the seven deadly sins
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven types of problematic interviewer moves to avoid so interviews can be constructive, informative, and respectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never: 1) Make a statement without a question (e.g., 'That was an annoying message.'); 2) Ask two questions at the same time; 3) Make a statement in a question ('You just lost your father; it must be hard!'); 4) Exaggerate in a question; 5) Use provocative or loaded terms; 6) Ask leading or rhetorical questions; 7) Ask closed questions (that limit response). These undermine learning and constructive conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview focusing on solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When interviewing about solutions, ask forward-looking 'What now?' questions and seek documentation proving effectiveness, scalability, and replicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key questions: What does it take to solve the problem? Who can solve it? Can you help solve it? Who is responsible? Do you know others who solved it? Why is it a good solution? Describe how it works and provide evidence. Ask about challenges and lessons others can learn. Apply equal critical pressure to 'heroes' proposing solutions as to 'villains'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview focusing on nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex issues, allow sources time and space to answer in detail, eliciting background, contradictions, context, doubts, and dilemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key questions: What is the background? How do you see the issue? Has it developed over time? Why is it difficult to agree or solve? What is the principal dilemma? Which actors are key? What collaboration might help? Which of opponent's arguments do you respect? What doubts do you have? What's going to happen now?

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive technique for live interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Special considerations for live TV/radio/social media interviews to maintain constructiveness while ensuring clarity and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches: Ask for solutions; ask heroes critical questions; ask about nuances and dilemmas. Determine angle clearly; avoid false balance; if interviewee avoids answering, ask why they have difficulty rather than repeating the same question aggressively; consider adding an introductory piece about a viable solution. Prepare audience-understandable questions and adapt technique to live constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted Pyramid with constructive twist
rubrics_metrics.description: Use classic inverted pyramid but include the final question 'What now?' to add a constructive angle and sense of anticipation/possible solution to the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with essentials (Who, What, Where, When, How, Why, What now?), then provide details and nice-to-know. Useful for brief clear reports; ending with 'what now' lends hope and constructive direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: CDP storytelling model (Core - Development - Perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: A model for constructive narratives: C = Core (problem and consequences); D = Development (historical development and journey, including turning points); P = Perspective (lessons, inspiration, alternative perspectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for personal formative stories or success stories; include turning points (T1, T2, ...) and show how inspiration/perspectives help the journey from problem to solution. Can be used for non-linear narratives when nuance and multiple perspectives are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change newsroom culture: phased transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-phase approach to adopt constructive journalism across a newsroom: Phase I Introduction, Phase II Idea Development, Phase III Decisive Phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phase I: gather audience feedback (e.g., questionnaires), train all staff in constructive journalism. Phase II: involve all employees in defining constructive journalism and devising formats; weekly meetings to develop ideas and 'DNA' for teams. Phase III: implement intensive production (series), give ownership to practitioners, allow room to fail, and document/process changes with external advisors if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain change: ongoing input and practical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain momentum after initial rollout via ambassadors, format groups, visual symbols, practical goals, and evidence of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create internal ambassador groups (journalists, photographers, designers), work on new formats (live debates), display visual reminders (Constructive Compass, CDP), set practical production goals, communicate evidence of audience response, and be persistent. Top challenges include involvement/enthusiasm among editors, maintaining goals, and resistance from traditional journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: SNIC – The Constructive Compass (Solution-Oriented, Nuanced, Involving, Critical)
rubrics_metrics.description: A daily editorial tool offering four starting directions: S = Solution-oriented; N = Nuanced overview; I = Involving citizens/stakeholders; C = Critical enquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SNIC in editorial meetings to guide story idea development. Not every story needs all four directions; some projects may explore multiple directions. Principles include building on concrete documented problems and testing solutions; portraying subtleties and giving overviews; inspiring, engaging, activating and listening to audiences so they recognize themselves; and maintaining critical enquiry within constructive work.
